name: KinoWASM (KinoRuntime)
baseline: WAMR iwasm fast interpreter (also compared against wasm3)
workload: CoreMark 1.0 compiled to a WASI wasm module (Clang 11.0.0, -O3) and a recursive fibonacci(40) module, each run through the runtime's own CLI; interpreter versus interpreter.
claimed_speedup: CoreMark Iterations/Sec: KinoRuntime 4385.746651, wasm3 3555.555556, iwasm (WAMR fast interpreter) 1734.417344; page states approximately 1.23x wasm3 and 2.53x iwasm. fibonacci(40): KinoRuntime 1838.94 ms, wasm3 2601.12 ms, iwasm 4298.94 ms; page states approximately 1.41x wasm3 and 2.34x iwasm.
compiler_and_flags: Guest module: Clang 11.0.0 (LLVM 176249bd6732), -O3. Runtime executables: KinoRuntime 'standard Clang build' with compiler version and preset not recorded; wasm3 version and build configuration not recorded; iwasm in fast-interpreter mode. Public build needs MSVC 14.50+ or clang-cl (guaranteed tail calls via musttail) with AVX2 enabled.
stars_or_usage: 0 stars; the README says it ships in several production console titles (console integrations are private)
tradeoffs: Interpreter (register-TOS, direct-threaded, tail calls), so far slower than JIT/AOT engines such as wasmtime or wasmer. Public repo builds only for Windows x64 and needs a compiler with guaranteed tail calls. No SIMD execution, no threads/atomics, no GC; WASI only partial; memory64 and exception handling partial. Host-controlled suspend/resume of guest execution is a feature. Embedding needs a host-provided linear-memory backend.
caveats: benchmark.md calls the numbers 'user-supplied measurements' and a 'preliminary snapshot': only one machine, runtime versions and compiler flags not recorded, workload binaries and CoreMark not bundled, iwasm ran 30,000 iterations while the other two ran 60,000, and the final CRC differs between iwasm (0x5275) and wasm3/KinoRuntime (0xbd59). The page itself says the metadata is insufficient for a fully documented CoreMark result. Fibonacci timing uses the in-guest clock via the runtime's WASI clock. wasm3 on Windows may be disadvantaged by its calling convention (the stitch README makes that claim for its own Windows numbers). Project is very new (first commit 2026-09-30, about 6 commits) and written by one person.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/webassembly-runtime?l=c (C language filter), then README and docs/benchmark.md

name: wasman
baseline: wazero v1.12 (interpreter mode and compiler mode); also wagon v0.4 and life
workload: Go benchmarks over tiny hand-written .wat modules: Fib(20) recursive, 100k-iteration Sum loop, 64KiB MemRW, module Instantiate (decode+validate+instantiate), plus JIT-mode kernels Sort (10k i32 quicksort), Dispatch (br_table), Hash, Mandel, Indirect (call_indirect).
claimed_speedup: Interpreter vs wazero interpreter (Apple M3, ns/op): Fib 974,787 vs 1,787,663; Sum 3,014,618 vs 3,930,498; MemRW 4,751,546 vs 5,153,545; Instantiate 2,129 vs 14,100; README says 1.1-1.8x faster than wazero's interpreter, 1.5-2.4x faster than wagon, about 2x faster than life, instantiation 3-14x faster. JIT vs wazero compiler: MemRW 39,575 vs 70,643, Sort 367,952 vs 477,368, Sum 27,112 vs 26,850 (level), Fib 41,187 vs 37,832 (slower), Indirect 3,926,713 vs 2,812,512 (1.4x slower); on dual EPYC 7K62 Sum 2.0x and MemRW 1.6x ahead of wazero compiler, Fib 1.6x behind.
compiler_and_flags: Go 1.24; go test -bench . -benchmem ./bench (default Go flags); fixtures compiled from .wat with wat2wasm and checked in; every run checked for the correct result before timing.
hardware: Apple M3 (main tables); dual AMD EPYC 7K62 server for the amd64 JIT comparison
tradeoffs: Pure Go with zero dependencies (no cgo), interpreter by default; optional tiered JIT (EnableJIT) only on arm64 and amd64 and per-function interpreter fallback (optimizing tier covers about 86% of spec-suite function bodies). The README claims full official spec-suite conformance, metering and interruption support.
caveats: Self-benchmarked by the project author; single run per row (no variance reported); very small workloads (Fib(20) is about 13k calls), so results may not transfer to real modules. Only Go engines were compared: cgo runtimes (wasmtime-go, wasmer-go) were deliberately excluded, so there is no comparison with wasmtime, wasmer, V8 or WAMR. The JIT result is mixed: ahead of wazero's compiler on memory-bound code, level on arithmetic, behind on recursion and call_indirect. Wazero is the Go incumbent but not one of the listed baselines.
found_via: GitHub: github.com/topics/wasm-runtime?l=go (Go language filter), then README Performance section and bench/README.md

name: WAVM (libsodium WebAssembly runtime benchmark, 2021-Q1)
baseline: wasmer (LLVM, Cranelift and singlepass backends), wasmtime, V8 (Node.js), lucet, Second State VM
workload: libsodium 1.0.18-stable built-in benchmark suite (cryptographic primitives and codecs) compiled to WASI wasm, the same pre-optimized .wasm run on every runtime; macOS and Linux x86_64 rounds.
claimed_speedup: 'WAVM remains the fastest WebAssembly runtime, beating the competition in every single test.' 'WAVM was still about 15% faster than wasmer' (LLVM backend); on the Linux/x86_64 LLVM round 'wavm remains undethroned' with SSVM coming 'really close'. Results are shown as PNG charts and raw files in 2021-Q1/output, no numeric table in the README.
compiler_and_flags: libsodium ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench; system compiler LLVM 11.1.0 (Homebrew) with default optimization flags, output pre-optimized with wasm-opt -O4; runtimes compiled from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode (Node.js stock package); wasm and native builds used the same default flags.
hardware: Intel CPU on macOS and a separate Linux/x86_64 machine; CPU models not stated (an ARM-based CPU was used for a separate aarch64 round that excluded WAVM)
stars_or_usage: 2.8k stars; benchmark repo jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks has 81 stars and was archived on 2026-08-19
tradeoffs: LLVM-based, so compile times are long (the EOS VM README calls WAVM's compilation times 'extremely long and unpredictable'). WAVM does not ship pre-compiled binaries for aarch64, so the author could not benchmark it on ARM; it was therefore not tested on ARM in this suite.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. Numbers are from February 2021 runtime snapshots and are stale; CPU model is not stated and individual tables are only PNG charts or output files; one author ran the suite. A later 2022-12 round exists in the same repo but its folder holds only pics/res/wasm directories and was not read. Newer 2026 runs of the same suite by the same author were seen only as search snippets (not opened), so they are not cited here.

name: wasm3 (libsodium WebAssembly runtime benchmark, 2021-Q1)
baseline: WAMR (Intel wasm-micro-runtime iwasm) in 'fast interpreter' mode
workload: libsodium 1.0.18-stable built-in benchmark suite compiled to WASI wasm (same .wasm for all runtimes), interpreter round on macOS (Intel) plus an aarch64 round.
claimed_speedup: 'wamr was slower than wasm3 on every single test.' Native code is 'about 30 times faster than wasm3' versus 'about 46 times faster' than wamr; on aarch64 wasm3 runs at 'about 3% of native speed'. Charts only, no numeric table in the README.
compiler_and_flags: libsodium ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench; LLVM 11.1.0 with default optimization flags, output pre-optimized with wasm-opt -O4; runtimes built from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode.
hardware: Intel CPU on macOS (model not stated); an ARM-based CPU for the aarch64 round (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Interpreter, so roughly 30x slower than native on this suite and far behind JIT/AOT runtimes; very small footprint (the benchmark author cites about 64Kb code and about 10Kb RAM). The README says wasm3 is entering a minimal maintenance phase.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. February 2021 snapshot: WAMR's fast interpreter was brand new then and has since been reworked, and wasm3 has changed too. CPU models not stated, results are PNG charts, single author. Only WAMR's interpreter mode was tested (not its AOT or JIT).
found_via: WebSearch 'WebAssembly runtime "faster than wasmtime" ...' surfaced the 00f.net benchmark series; opened github.com/jedisct1/webassembly-benchmarks 2021-Q1 README

name: V8 (libsodium WebAssembly runtime benchmark, 2021-Q1)
baseline: wasmer (Cranelift, singlepass, LLVM backends), wasmtime, lucet
workload: libsodium 1.0.18-stable built-in benchmark suite compiled to WASI wasm, run through Node.js's experimental WASI; macOS (Intel) round.
claimed_speedup: 'V8 (nodejs) being the second top performer was quite of a surprise', behind WAVM and ahead of wasmer and wasmtime on the Intel macOS charts; author's verdict 'Just use NodeJS'. On the aarch64 round Node ran at 'around 49% the speed of native code' versus wasmtime at '~54%' (so wasmtime was ahead there).
compiler_and_flags: libsodium ./dist/wasm32-wasi.sh --bench; LLVM 11.1.0 default flags plus wasm-opt -O4; Node.js installed from stock precompiled packages (version not stated); other runtimes built from git on 2021-02-21 in release mode.
hardware: Intel CPU on macOS (model not stated); an ARM-based CPU for the aarch64 round (model not stated)
tradeoffs: Full browser-grade engine (Liftoff baseline plus TurboFan), large dependency and memory footprint; the benchmark author notes Node's memory use may be higher than alternatives and that Node's WASI was still experimental.
caveats: Evidence for an already catalogued project. 2021 snapshot with an unspecified Node.js version; wasmtime and wasmer have changed a lot since. V8 is not the winner on aarch64 in the same page. CPU models not stated, charts only, single author.
